pages.title: Your First Website in Lombard, IL | Project Knox
pages.metaDescription: Website design in Lombard, IL for a business starting from nothing. Your own domain, email to match, and a site that says plainly what you sell and charge.
pages.h1: Website design in Lombard, IL, when you're starting with a phone number and not much else.
pages.lede: No site, a Google listing you've never once logged into, and a number painted on a sign. That's a normal place to begin, and it's where most of our builds start.

sections.h2: A Facebook page is an address on somebody else's land.
paras: Plenty of good businesses around here run entirely off one. The hours are inside a post from March, the price list is a photograph of a printed sheet, and the messages land in an inbox that buzzes on a phone in an apron pocket. It works, right up until you need to be found by somebody who isn't already searching for you by name.

What a page can't do is the problem. It can't be your address in an email signature. It can't put your services in front of a stranger deciding at ten at night. It doesn't choose how it looks, what sits beside it, or whether it still exists in three years. Keep it, because it's doing real work — just stop letting it be the entire business.

sections.h2: Six lines a first website has to get right before anything else.
paras: You don't need twelve pages. You need the answers people already call to ask, arranged in the order they ask them.
bullets: What you do, said in the words a customer would use rather than the ones on your license
Where you are, or how far you travel, with a map that opens in a single tap
When you're open, including whatever the honest answer is about Sundays
What it costs, or at minimum a range and the thing that moves it
How to reach a person — a number that dials when tapped, and a form that actually arrives
Proof the place is real: the room, the truck, the work, and you

sections.h2: The domain and the email come before the pretty part.
paras: A domain registered to you is the first thing you own online that nobody else can suspend, redesign or change the rules on. We buy it into your account rather than ours, along with the Google Business Profile and the customer list, and all three stay in your name whatever happens between us.

Email arrives with the domain. Google Workspace runs it, which means the address a customer hits reply on ends in your own name rather than somebody else's. That reads differently to a stranger deciding whether to hand you money, and doing it right costs nothing extra at the start. The calendar and the shared drive come along, and the booking page writes into that same calendar.

sections.h2: The photographs already on your phone beat anything we could buy.
paras: Stock photography is the tell. A visitor can't explain why the page feels off, but they have seen that same smiling crew on four other sites this month, and something in them files you under businesses that might not exist.

Send what you have. The bay halfway through a job, the lawn once it's finished, the counter at ten past eight in the morning, your own hands doing the thing you do. Slightly blurry beats borrowed. We crop, size and place them, and we'll tell you which three are worth taking again on a bright morning.

sections.h2: It has to load before a stranger gives up on it.
paras: Somebody who has never heard of you grants the page a second or two without ever knowing they did it. If nothing useful has appeared by then, the thumb goes back to the results and tries the next name, and none of that reaches you as feedback you could learn from.

So the pages are mostly text and images cut to the size of the slot they sit in, with no page-builder software layered underneath multiplying the weight. Nothing shifts under a finger as things settle. Your number can be tapped before the top photograph has finished arriving, and the whole thing behaves the same on a five-year-old handset.

sections.h2: Two changes a month, because a first year changes constantly.
paras: New businesses rewrite themselves. Prices move once you've done the job twenty times, a service gets dropped because nobody wanted it, the hours settle into what genuinely works, and quite often the thing you thought you sold turns out to be second to something you barely mentioned.

Send us the change and it gets made. Two of them a month come with the plan, and asking is the only step involved — nobody opens a ticket, nobody issues a change order, nobody schedules a call about one paragraph. That matters more in your first year than it ever will later, which is why it's on this page rather than buried in a plan comparison.

sections.h2: If money is tight this month, here is the honest advice.
paras: Foundation is priced at $250 a month, with $250 once at the start, across a twelve-month term. If you're still finding out whether the business itself holds together, that's a genuine commitment and we'd rather say so now than let you work it out in month four.

Squarespace is inexpensive and it's good. If you like fiddling with that sort of thing on a Sunday evening, you'll do fine on it. What it hands back to you is everything surrounding the site: claiming the profile, writing every page, sizing every image, keeping hours truthful, wiring up booking, and repairing whatever breaks in the week you can least spare an evening. Read that list and work out which is scarcer for you at the moment, the money or the evenings.

pages.townPara: Yorktown Center opened in 1968 and was once counted the second-largest enclosed mall east of the Mississippi — roughly 1.5 million square feet of retail sitting inside one village. North Avenue runs its own version of the same idea. So a small business starting up here opens in the same village as an enormous amount of professional signage, professional lighting and professional everything else. You aren't going to outspend that and you don't need to. The searches you can genuinely win are narrow ones, made nearby by somebody who wants precisely what you do, and those get decided on a page rather than on a frontage.

crmCallout.heading: Later, the site should start keeping the records for you.
crmCallout.para: 'CRM' is only a name for the place customer information lives — the enquiry, the booking, the invoice, the person due back in six weeks. On Foundation the site brings people to your door and you handle what follows however you handle it today. On Growth, $500 a month with a $500 setup, the site and the records are one system, so a form filled in at midnight is already a contact with a history forming behind it. Begin with whichever half hurts more; adding the other later switches on parts that were built in from the start.

cta.heading: Nothing behind this door is a mockup, so go and use one.
cta.para: Six businesses sit behind that door, each finished the whole way through, and no two of them are in the same trade. Open whichever sits closest to your trade, click every link in it, and decide whether it reads like a working business or a brochure. Then call (331) 291-7400 and tell us what yours would need to say.

faqs.q: I don't have a domain, a logo or any photographs. Is that a problem?
faqs.a: It's the ordinary starting point and it slows nothing down. We register the domain in your name, set up email at it, and build from whatever you can photograph on your phone this week. A logo isn't required to launch and can be added later without touching the rest — plenty of trades do better with a clear name set in good type than with a hurried logo.

faqs.q: Why twelve months when I'm only just starting out?
faqs.a: Because a website takes around three months to begin earning its keep, and an agreement built to be canceled quickly tends to be built cheaply too. We'd rather make the thing that works. There's a year of our time going into it from this side as well, which is the part that usually goes unsaid.

faqs.q: What does the first site cost, all in?
faqs.a: Foundation asks $250 each month, plus $250 once at the beginning. Inside that figure: the site, the domain held in your name, Google Workspace email, the Google Business Profile, booking wired to your calendar, the search work, and two changes a month whenever you want them. Growth is the version with a ledger behind it, holding the invoices, the card payments, the messages that go out on their own and the asking for reviews. That one runs $500 a month after a $500 setup. Pay a year ahead and 15% comes off, bringing the twelve months to $2,550 or $5,100, setup excluded.

pages.formHeading: Tell us what you sell and who buys it.
pages.formSub: Two lines is plenty to work from, and a real person reads it and writes back inside a day.

pages.title: Getting Found in Lombard, IL | Project Knox
pages.metaDescription: Local SEO in Lombard, IL for a business Google barely knows. We claim and build out the Google Business Profile, write real service pages, get reviews moving.
pages.h1: Local SEO in Lombard, IL, for a business Google doesn't know exists yet.
pages.lede: Ranking badly and being absent altogether are two different problems. Most new businesses have the second one, and it's a shorter job than it sounds.

sections.h2: There's probably a listing for you already, and you've never seen it.
paras: Google assembles listings out of whatever it can find — a supplier directory, a permit, a licence record, somebody adding a shop while staring at a map. So a version of your business may be sitting out there right now with a wrong closing time, your name spelled the way somebody guessed it and no photographs at all, answering questions on your behalf while you get on with the work.

Claiming it puts you in charge of what people are already being shown. Verification is usually a postcard, a call or a short video walk of the premises, depending on what Google asks of your category. It's the highest-value afternoon on this whole page, and until it's done the rest of the search work is pushing on a locked door.

sections.h2: When everything is missing at once, the order matters.
paras: Owners starting from zero tend to do the interesting parts first and the load-bearing parts never. So there's a sequence, and we work through it in this order.
bullets: Week one: the profile claimed and verified, the primary category chosen deliberately, the name, address and number saying one identical thing everywhere
Week two: the site live, with a separate page for each service you want more of rather than a single list of nine
Week three: photographs of the real place, every hour including the awkward ones, and the questions people phone up to ask answered in writing
From then on: a request behind every finished job, every review answered, and one page written or rewritten each month

sections.h2: The first ten reviews are the hardest and the most valuable.
paras: A profile with nothing under it reads as either brand new or quietly closed, and a stranger can't tell which. Ten honest reviews settle that question outright. After ten it stops being a milestone and becomes a habit that runs in the background.

So the asking gets built into the job instead of relying on you remembering during a rush. One message goes out behind each completed piece of work, the same wording for everybody, and nobody gets chased a second time. On Growth that runs by itself. Before then, do it by hand for two weeks and you'll see the effect for yourself.

Never buy them, never write them yourself, and never offer anything in exchange for one. It breaks Google's rules, customers can smell it from a distance, and a wall of perfect scores on a two-month-old business achieves the opposite of what you were hoping for.

sections.h2: Your name, address and number have to agree with each other.
paras: Somewhere out there is an old suite number, a mobile you stopped answering, and a version of your name using an ampersand where the sign says the word. Google reads all of it while working out whether you're one business or three, and a business it can't pin down is one it shows less often.
Tidying that up is dull, invisible work with an actual finish line, which makes it rare in this field. It gets done once, thoroughly, and then guarded whenever something about you changes.

sections.h2: Write for what gets typed, not for what goes on a sign.
paras: A sign carries your business name. A search carries the problem — somebody wants their gutters cleared, or a barber open on a Monday, or whatever the equivalent is in your trade at half past nine on a weeknight. Those two sets of words barely overlap, and only one of them is how new customers arrive.

So each service worth having more of gets a page to itself, written the way the thing is said out loud, with the town where it belongs and nowhere it doesn't. Underneath that sits structured data, spelling out your trade, your hours and the area you cover in a form a machine can read without interpreting a layout to get at it.

sections.h2: What we won't say, and what happens every week instead.
paras: Nobody sells position on that map. Google doesn't take money for placement in local results, so a guarantee of the top three is a promise about something the person making it doesn't control. Anyone offering you one is counting on you not checking.
In its place, here is the trade — named work, on a rhythm, written down and reported back.
bullets: The profile pushed forward every month rather than touched only when something breaks
Requests going out behind finished work, and every review that arrives answered in your voice
A page added or rewritten as you learn which services people are really ringing about
Directories and listings kept saying one consistent thing about who you are and where you are
Page speed and dead links watched, since Google quietly stops showing a page that broke
A short written account each month of what we did and what it shifted, blank months included

sections.h2: The profile wakes up first. The website takes longer.
paras: Filling in a profile that was empty can show results within a few weeks, since you're handing Google facts it wanted anyway. A site earning trust is slower work — three months is a fair point at which to start judging it, and a crowded trade takes longer than that.
Expect the map to move before the pages do, and treat anybody promising it inside a month as somebody who has never done it.

pages.townPara: The whole village shares a single ZIP code, 60148, which quietly removes one of the crude signals a search engine might otherwise use to tell one end of Lombard from the other. Distance from whoever is searching still counts, and you can't move the shop. Everything else is yours to change: whether the profile is claimed, whether it's complete, whether it's active, and whether a page exists that says clearly what you sell. The Lombard Area Chamber of Commerce and Industry can put you in a room with other owners. It can't put you in a set of results, and that part is mechanical.

crmCallout.heading: The calls have to land somewhere better than a coat pocket.
crmCallout.para: A CRM is simply where customer information lives, and when you're new it earns its keep for a reason nobody mentions in the sales pitch: it tells you which of your first fifty customers came off the map, which came off a sign and which came from somebody's cousin. That's the difference between spending next year on what works and spending it on what merely felt busy. Growth carries it at $500 a month with a $500 setup, and the 24/7 automated answering bolt-on at $100 a month picks up whatever rings while both your hands are occupied.

cta.heading: Read a set of service pages written the way we mean it.
cta.para: Knox Blocks is a lawn and landscape business we built end to end, down to how each job is named and described. Read two of its pages, then call (331) 291-7400 and we'll look up what Google currently holds on you while you're still on the line.

faqs.q: There's a listing for my business on Google that I never made. What's that?
faqs.a: An unclaimed profile, built by Google out of public information. Anyone can suggest an edit to one, so the details drift and you never hear about it. You claim it rather than create a second one, since a duplicate splits your reviews and confuses the map. If duplicates already exist, closing them properly is part of the work.

faqs.q: I have no reviews at all. Where do the first ones come from?
faqs.a: From the customers you already served, asked once, in the hour while you're still fresh in mind. A short message with a direct link does most of it — people intend to leave one and then life happens, and the link is what turns intending into done. Ask everybody the same way and never filter who gets asked, because that last part is against the rules and it shows.

faqs.q: If the Google profile is doing the work, do I need the site as well?
faqs.a: The profile can carry you further than most people expect, and if you only ever do one thing, do that one. It has limits, though. It can't describe a service properly, it can't answer the four questions people ask before booking, and the list of links under the map is a race your profile isn't even entered in. The two feed each other, which is why they're in one plan rather than sold separately.

faqs.q: How long before we start showing up for anything?
faqs.a: Profile work can register in weeks. Pages take about three months to be worth judging, and longer where several established businesses are already competing for the same three pins. What you should see early is the map listing looking complete and active, which is what earns the first calls while the slower half is still building.

faqs.q: Does this cost extra once the site is built?
faqs.a: No. It's inside Foundation, which runs $250 a month after $250 at the start, and that one figure also carries the site, the email, the profile and the booking page. Move up to Growth — $500 a month, $500 to begin — and the review requests come with it, along with the ledger they write into. Nobody turns up later with a second retainer, and no ad spend is being quietly assumed underneath the number.

pages.formHeading: Tell us what you want the calls for.
pages.formSub: Say which job you want the calls for and how far it has to travel, and we'll tell you where you sit on that search right now.

pages.title: CRM & Follow-Up in Lombard, IL | Project Knox
pages.metaDescription: The CRM for a Lombard, IL business: one inbox for enquiries, booking on your calendar, follow-up, invoicing, expenses, QuickBooks sync and monthly reports.
pages.h1: A CRM for a Lombard, IL business, starting with the enquiries nobody got back to.
pages.lede: 'CRM' is a three-letter way of saying the place where everything you know about a customer is kept. Built properly it catches the enquiry, takes the booking, sends the reminder and notices the regular who quietly stopped coming — and it belongs to Growth at $500 a month plus a one-time $500 setup.

sections.h2: The enquiries arrive in five places and get answered in about three.
paras: A message on the Facebook page. A text to your personal number. A voicemail. A note somebody wrote on the back of a card. An email you read at a red light and fully intended to come back to. Every one of those was a person who, at that moment, was ready to give you money.

None of them get lost on purpose. They get lost because there's nowhere they were ever supposed to be, so "did anyone ever get back to her" is a question with no way of being answered. During a good week the true answer is often no, and you never learn it, because somebody who hears nothing doesn't complain. They simply go quiet and you assume they were never serious.

One place for the lot is the first thing this fixes. Each enquiry becomes a record carrying a name, a number, where it came from and whether it has been dealt with, and anything unanswered stays in front of you until somebody deals with it.

sections.h2: Booking that doesn't need you free to have a conversation.
paras: The booking page reads the Google Calendar you already carry, so whatever you put on it privately — a school pickup, a delivery window, a morning you're taking back for yourself — stops being offered to the public. Nothing needs copying anywhere else, because a second diary never comes into existence.

For somebody who has never had this, the change is that phone tag ends. A customer calls while you're mid-job, they leave no message, you call back at ten to seven and they're eating dinner, and somewhere inside that gap they booked with whoever answered on the first attempt. That costs you the work and the twenty minutes of calling back you did anyway.

What lands is the name, the number, the job and the hour, and the customer hears back without you writing a word. A booking made at eleven at night is on the calendar before you wake up, spelled correctly, with the service already attached to it.

sections.h2: The regular who quietly stopped coming.
paras: Nothing happens when you lose one, which is exactly why it goes unnoticed. There's no cancellation and no complaint. Somebody who came every six weeks for two years just isn't there in week seven, or week nine, and by the time it registers she has been going somewhere else since spring.

What that cost wasn't one appointment. It was every appointment she'd have made for the rest of the year, and in most cases she'd have stayed if a single person had noticed in week eight and said something.

The ledger knows her interval because it watched her keep it. Once she is past it she appears on a list with her number beside her, or a short note goes out on its own asking whether she wants her usual time. A good share of those people were only busy. A few have moved on and will tell you so, which is worth knowing as well.

sections.h2: The one who asked the price and then went quiet.
paras: Every business has a pile of these and no way of seeing the size of it. Somebody called in April, asked a couple of questions, said they'd speak to their husband about it, and that was the end. You can picture two of them. There were thirty.

Almost none were a no. They were a maybe with nothing behind it to keep the maybe alive, and a maybe left alone becomes a decision made elsewhere. One message a few weeks later does most of the work: the price still stands, there's room in the next couple of weeks, and if the timing is wrong you'll leave them in peace.

Nothing currently competes with this, because nothing currently happens. People who didn't buy leave no trace at all, so the loss never lands on a report — and the size of that list is what surprises owners most on the first month they can finally see it.

sections.h2: The texts you'd send if you had the time.
paras: Three of them do most of the work. A reminder the day before. A thank-you once they're back in the car. A check-in at whatever gap your trade runs on, whether that's six weeks, six months or every March. Each gets written once and then goes out carrying the right name and the right time without you touching it.

The reminder pays for itself first, because an empty two o'clock can't be sold to anybody afterwards at any price. The thank-you carries the review request, and for a business with no reviews yet that single line does more than anything else described here.

None of it should read like software. We write them the way you actually talk and you sign each one off before it goes anywhere near a customer, because a message that's obviously automatic reads as being handled by a machine — which is the one impression a small local business genuinely can't afford.

sections.h2: Invoices and card payments, once the customer side is working.
paras: An invoice assembles itself out of the appointment already in the system — name, date, service, price — and goes out by text or email with a link that takes a card. Cash and checks carry on working precisely as they do now. This is a route added, not a habit taken away.

Payments record against the person rather than in a separate history somewhere else, so what was billed, what has been paid and what's still open sits on one screen per customer. Deposits work through the same connection, which is the usual answer to being burned on the jobs that block out a whole morning.

This sits sixth on the page on purpose. Early on, the money side is still small enough to hold in your head. The customer side isn't, and it's the half that decides whether there's a second year to do the accounting for.

sections.h2: Receipts go in where you're standing, and the books stay current.
paras: Money going out gets written down beside money coming in. Photograph the receipt in the lot — fuel, materials, the tool you had to buy at eight in the morning, the flyers you had run off — and it's dated, categorized and filed against the work before you've climbed back into the van.

The alternative is a glovebox, a coat pocket and one ruined weekend a year. Paper that faded on a dashboard is tax you never owed and paid anyway, and in a first or second year that money is worth more to you than it ever will be later.

All of it syncs to QuickBooks, or to whatever your accountant prefers to work in, arriving already sorted so nobody re-types numbers that were typed once. If you haven't hired an accountant yet, this is the thing that makes hiring one cheap — handing over books that are current costs a fraction of handing over a box of loose paper, and you get quoted accordingly.

sections.h2: One page of numbers, emailed on the first.
paras: The report comes to you rather than waiting behind a login. That distinction sounds trivial and isn't, because a dashboard you have to remember to open is a dashboard you'll open twice and then forget about.
bullets: What came in, split by service, so it's obvious which work is carrying you
What went out, by category, with the previous month set beside it
Who is overdue for a visit, listed by name with a number
How many customers were new against how many came back
What's still unpaid, and how long it has been that way

sections.h2: What it costs, and what the cheaper plan won't do.
paras: All of it sits inside Growth: $500 each month, and $500 once, at the beginning. That figure includes the website standing in front of it, the profile, the email at your domain and the search work — it isn't an add-on price sitting on top of a website price.

Foundation, at $250 a month with a $250 setup, contains none of this page. Better you have that from a page you can re-read than from somebody talking fast on a phone. Foundation is the getting-found half, and for a business with no site and an unclaimed profile that's frequently the right thing to buy first.

A year paid up front takes 15% off — $2,550 on Foundation, $5,100 on Growth, working out at $212.50 and $425 a month, with setup billed separately. Two extras can sit on top of whichever plan you pick: phone answering around the clock for $100 a month, and automated replies to your Google reviews for $130. Work outside all that gets quoted on its own, in writing, before anybody begins it.

The term is a year, and the bill arrives on the same date each month. The reason is the one we give everybody: three months is roughly how long a site takes to begin paying for itself, and a shorter agreement mostly buys a cheaper build.
bullets: The full Foundation build, with a ledger sitting under every part of it
One inbox for calls, forms, texts and messages, and nothing unanswered hiding in a pocket
Booking on the calendar you already carry, with confirmations and reminders attached
Follow-up for customers who lapsed and for enquiries that never became work
Invoicing, card payments, deposits, and everything outstanding on a single screen
Receipts captured from your phone, accounting kept in step, and the monthly page of numbers

pages.townPara: The village holds 44,476 people and has a tollway along two of its edges — I-355 to the west, I-88 to the south. That shape does something particular to a small business here. Some of your customers are neighbors who will walk in and know your first name within a month. Others are passing through a place they don't live in, will never see your sign, and choose you once. A number on a door serves the first group perfectly well. Only a record that keeps track of everybody — how they found you, when they were last in, what they still owe — serves both, and most owners discover the second group far too late.

crmCallout.heading: The list is yours from the very first name written into it.
crmCallout.para: The names in that ledger are yours. So is the domain, and so is the Google Business Profile — all three go into your account in week one, not into ours. Walk away and they walk with you, exported into a file any other system will read, with nothing to wait out and nobody calling to talk you round. It's worth saying plainly, because a fair amount of this trade is arranged so that going elsewhere costs an owner the very people the business was built on.

cta.heading: Open it and go looking for the customer you'd have forgotten.
cta.para: What's behind the link is live, loaded up with a year of somebody's trading. Put an appointment on the calendar, send yourself an invoice, open a customer record, read the list of people who are overdue and see whether that list looks like your year. After that, (331) 291-7400 reaches a person, and so does the form below, and we can talk about where your enquiries are landing at the moment.

faqs.q: We have never had a system at all. What happens to the customers in my phone?
faqs.a: They come across. Contacts from a phone, a spreadsheet, an old booking app or a card reader's history are an import rather than a retype. A paper book is the awkward case, and there we normally bring over whoever is still active and leave the rest in the drawer, because a hundred names you'll never contact again aren't worth an evening of typing.

faqs.q: Can I start on Foundation and add the CRM later?
faqs.a: Yes, and quite a few businesses should. Get found first, get the phone ringing, then turn on the thing that catches what the ringing produces. Moving up isn't a rebuild and nothing gets thrown away — it's the same system with more of it running, and the difference on the bill is the difference between the two plans.

faqs.q: What does the CRM cost on top of the website?
faqs.a: Nothing on top. It's Growth at $500 a month with a one-time $500 setup, and that single figure covers both the ledger and the site in front of it. Settled twelve months in advance it becomes $5,100 for the year, an effective $425 a month, and setup stays on its own line. The two bolt-ons stay optional at $100 and $130 a month.

faqs.q: Will automated texts make us sound like a big company?
faqs.a: They will if somebody else writes them. We draft each message in the way you speak, you approve every one before it's switched on, and they go out signed by your business rather than by a system. The test we use is simple enough: if you'd be uncomfortable saying that sentence across a counter, it doesn't go out.

faqs.q: What happens to all of it if this doesn't work out between us?
faqs.a: All three of those things went into your name at the start, so nothing changes hands when we stop. The list comes out as a file anything else can open, and there's no notice period standing between you and it. You would leave with a working business rather than a hole where one had been.

pages.formHeading: Tell us where the enquiries land now.
pages.formSub: Phone, texts, messages, a note by the register, or all four at once — say which, and a real person reads it and answers inside a day.

pages.title: Take Bookings Online in Lombard, IL | Project Knox
pages.metaDescription: Online booking and payments in Lombard, IL for a business run off one phone. Times get claimed on a page, reminders go out alone, deposits clear in advance.
pages.h1: Online booking and payments in Lombard, IL, when everything currently runs through your phone.
pages.lede: A number on a sign only works during the hours somebody can pick it up. The rest of the time it's a small test your customer decides not to take.

sections.h2: A fair share of the people who want you won't call you.
paras: This is the part owners argue with, and it's the easiest claim on the page to check. Think about how you booked the last haircut, table or appointment you made for yourself. Calling a stranger and negotiating a time out loud has quietly become a task most people will avoid if any other route exists, and where none exists they find somebody who offers one.

That isn't everybody, and nothing here takes the phone away — plenty of your customers will always want to hear a voice. What a booking page does is stop you losing the ones who were never going to call in the first place, at ten at night, on a Sunday, or while both of your hands were inside somebody else's job.

sections.h2: The calendar has to become real before any of this works.
paras: Businesses at this stage usually keep the diary in one of three places: a paper book beside the register, the notes app, or somebody's head. None of the three can be read by a website, so the first move is onto a Google Calendar that lives on every device you own and gets checked by everybody who needs it.

That calendar comes with the email included in your plan, so it isn't another subscription to find. Once it's the only copy, the booking page both reads it and writes to it, and any hours you block out for something else simply stop being offered to anyone.

sections.h2: Put two services on the page to begin with, not eleven.
paras: The temptation with a new booking page is to list everything you're capable of doing. It makes the page long, it makes choosing hard, and it gets you booked for exactly the jobs you're least confident about timing.

So it opens with the two or three you could price and schedule in your sleep, each with a truthful duration, a gap behind it for clearing up, and a rule about how soon somebody may claim a slot. Everything else stays behind an enquiry form until you know its shape well enough to sell it while you aren't in the room. Services move from one side to the other as you learn, and that's the normal course of a first year rather than a sign anything went wrong.

sections.h2: The confirmation and the reminder are texts you stop having to write.
paras: The confirmation is immediate, and it's the one claim here you can verify in about a minute — make a booking in the barbershop demo and watch what turns up in your own inbox.

After that comes the day-before reminder with the time and the address inside it. Between them, those two messages remove most of the back-and-forth texting that currently eats an hour of your evening, and most of the people who would otherwise have simply forgotten. On Growth they run automatically, along with the thank-you afterwards.

sections.h2: Taking a card when you've never taken one online.
paras: Deposits exist for one reason. The slot is the only thing you actually sell, and somebody who doesn't appear has taken it out of your day and handed you nothing back. A card taken at the moment of booking filters for intention, and the filtering happens quietly, before it has cost you a morning.

The same connection handles an order placed on the site, a link inside a text, and a card run at the counter, with all three recording against the person who paid rather than living in a separate app you check at closing time. Taking cards is a Growth feature, at $500 a month after a $500 setup. Booking that writes to your calendar arrives earlier, in Foundation, which is $250 a month after $250 at the outset.

sections.h2: In a year you'll want to know who booked what, and when.
paras: For the first few months a booking page is about convenience. Give it a year and it becomes history — how often that customer comes, what she has spent with you, whether she is late, which services bring people back and which ones nobody ever repeats.
That's what the ledger underneath is for, and it's the reason we'd rather set the calendar up carefully at the start than tidy up twelve months of half-kept records afterwards.

pages.townPara: Look at what a village actually schedules itself around. Helen Plum Library is one of those places and Glenbard East is another, and between them they account for a good share of where people in Lombard have to be on a weekday evening. Arrangements get made in the gaps left over — sitting in a car outside a school, standing in line somewhere, at half nine at night once the house has finally gone quiet. Those are exactly the hours your phone goes unanswered and your door is locked, and they are the hours a booking page is paid to cover.

crmCallout.heading: The booking page is the cheapest way to start keeping records.
crmCallout.para: 'CRM' is only the name for wherever customer information ends up living, and for most businesses at this stage that's a phone and a memory. Every appointment taken online writes a line of a proper one without anybody doing data entry — who, what, when, how much, and how they found you. Growth carries the rest of it, from invoices through to follow-up, expenses and the monthly page of numbers, at $500 a month with a one-time $500 setup.

cta.heading: Book something in a demo and watch the whole loop close.
cta.para: Knox Nails is a complete salon we built, booking included. Choose a time, wait for the confirmation to arrive, then work out what those same thirty seconds would be worth across a Saturday of yours. When it makes sense, call (331) 291-7400.

faqs.q: I'm not much good with computers. Is running this going to be my job?
faqs.a: No. We set the services, the durations, the gaps and the rules with you at the start, and after that the only thing you touch is your own calendar — the same one on your phone. Changes to prices or hours are something you ask us for, and they're included. Nobody hands you an admin panel and wishes you luck.

faqs.q: What stops two people booking the same time?
faqs.a: The page offers only what the calendar says is free, and a slot is held the moment somebody starts confirming it, so the second person never sees it as available. Anything you add to your calendar by hand closes those hours immediately. The failure people fear comes from systems keeping a diary of their own, and this one doesn't keep a second diary.

faqs.q: What do booking and payments come to?
faqs.a: The booking half is Foundation work: $250 monthly, and $250 once. Card payments, the messages that go out by themselves and the records all of it writes into are Growth, which runs $500 monthly after $500 at the start. Pay for the year at once and 15% comes off, making it $2,550 or $5,100, with setup billed apart from that.
